* * * [In Allied-Signal, Inc. v. U.S. Nuclear Regulatory Common, 
988 F.2d 146 (D.C. Cir. 1993)], the D.C. Circuit articulated a generic 
test for a practice that it had used sporadically in the past: remanding 
rules to agencies without vacating them. When a court remands a 
rule without vacating it, the agency can continue to implement the 
regulation while it addresses the defects in the regulation identijded 
by the reviewing court. As when rules are vacated, the agency can 
cure the defects by repromulgating the same rule with a different 
rationale or by promulgating a different rule.
Remand without vacatur (RWV) is controversial in the academic 
literature, both in terms of its effects in individual cases and in its 
systemic effects. At the individual case level, RWV can prevent the 
disruption of regulatory regimes that protect individuals against 
what can be serious risks to life and health. Commentators also view 
RWV as having positive systemic effects in providing a means to 
crack agency “ossification.” Ossification refers to agencies’ reluctance 
to undertake major rulemaking out of fear that their efforts will be 
nullified upon judicial review. By reducing the negative consequences 
of judicial review, RWV may help to encourage agencies to undertake 
comprehensive rulemaking in the first place. Commentators also 
have noted, however, that the regular use of RWV by courts may 
reduce the incentives for agencies to engage in carefully reasoned 
decisionmaking. * * *
The generic test in Allied-Signal, to which Daugirdas refers, says that the 
court’s “decision whether to vacate depends on ‘the seriousness of the [rulej’s 
deficiencies (and thus the extent of doubt whether the agency chose correctly) 
and the disruptive consequences of an interim change that may itself be 
changed’ ” Allied-Signal, 988 F.2d at 151 (citation omitted).
In re Core Communications, Inc., 531 F.3d 849 (D.C. Cir. 2008), illustrates 
why remand without vacatur may be problematic. The D.C. Circuit held in 
2002 that the FCC had failed to provide an adequate statutory basis for its 
promulgation of a certain rule. The court remanded the rule without vacating 
it, expecting the agency to come up with a new and better justification. Six 
years later, in 2008, the agency had not provided any new justification. The 
court therefore issued—at the behest of a company harmed by the as-yet- 
unjustified rule—a writ of mandamus, announcing that the rule would be 
vacated on a date certain, three months hence, unless the agency issued a new 
justification by then. Concurring, Judge Griffith pointed out that remand 
without vacatur “sometimes invites agency indifference.” He urged his 
colleagues, in future cases, to consider alternatives, such as attaching set 
deadlines to non-vacatur remands, or vacating while inviting motions to delay
